material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
At equal phase ratio, extractant X0 should give the strongest product recovery and best nominal product/impurity discrimination; X1 should sacrifice recovery while retaining discrimination. This prior comes only from the dossier and may be misindexed. A single-contact test predicts more target in the retained organic phase for X0 than X1 under matched conditions.

## H2 [tentative]
Reaction outcome likely depends categorically on catalyst and solvent plus temperature/time. I will screen category combinations, then repeat and refine the best purity-feasible region. The working objective is final recovery conditional on purity >= 0.80, not native score alone.

## Decision rule
Use early batches to identify a reaction/extraction recipe, then spend later batches on phase-ratio, washing, and repeatability. Revise if analytical evidence contradicts nominal extraction ordering.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [unresolved]
The dossier favors X0 for organic recovery/selectivity, but no matched extractant comparison has yet been completed. All completed batches retained organic and used X0, so the extraction prior remains untested rather than confirmed.

## H2 [supported in screened scope]
Reaction performance is strongly recipe-dependent. At 390 K/3600 s with catalyst C1 and split reagent/component charge, solvent S2 gave the best reaction-stage HPLC among S1–S3: event runner-operation-0089 reported higher purity, selectivity, and recovery than events runner-operation-0072 and runner-operation-0106. Differences are large relative to the stated single-measurement standard deviations, though recipes have not yet been replicated.

## H3 [tentative]
Catalyst C1/S2 is the current lead reaction recipe, but the final X0 organic workflow only reached assay purity about 0.778 and recovery about 0.105 (runner-operation-0100), just below the purity constraint. The next tests will screen other catalysts in S2 and then trade extraction/wash severity against recovery.

## Confound and decision
Early 350 K screens used only add_reagent whereas later 390 K screens split the charge between add_reagent and component, so temperature, charge mode, and solvent effects are not fully separable. Select future conditions by final purity-feasible recovery, and require a later repeat of the chosen complete workflow.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [unresolved]
The nominal X0 partition advantage was used throughout but never tested against another extractant. It is therefore a prior-guided choice, not an experimentally isolated extractant effect.

## H2 [supported in screened scope]
For the split reagent/component charge at 390 K and 3600 s, catalyst C1 with solvent S2 was the strongest reaction-stage region screened. HPLC events runner-operation-0089, runner-operation-0174, and runner-operation-0191 all showed materially higher reaction-stage recovery than the early 350 K recipes, though batch-to-batch variation and simultaneous design changes prevent a clean causal coefficient.

## H3 [revised: purity/recovery tradeoff unresolved]
The high-recovery C1/S2 complete workflows did not meet the final purity threshold: batch 6 reached recovery ~0.105 at purity ~0.778 (runner-operation-0100), while later wash/phase-ratio variants remained below 0.80 (runner-operation-0185 and runner-operation-0202). Batch 8 was numerically close at purity ~0.797 and recovery ~0.053 (runner-operation-0134), but the observed assay is below the stated constraint; it is not treated as feasible.

## Final decision
Among observed purity-feasible completed batches, batch 2 has the largest final recovery (~0.0077) with purity ~0.848 (runner-operation-0034), exceeding feasible batches 1 and 4 on recovery. I will recommend batch 2 despite its low absolute recovery. This is a constraint-respecting selection, not a claim that the underlying chemistry is optimized.

## Remaining alternatives
A future campaign should independently compare extractants, replicate the C1/S2 reaction before purification, and tune organic/aqueous ratio plus wash severity with more than one downstream assay. The present campaign cannot resolve whether the near-threshold failures reflect process variability or systematic selectivity limits.

payload.report:
Mechanism report

1. Scope and evidence

This account describes only the anonymous synthetic benchmark studied in the 12 completed batches. Material indices are categories, not real chemical identities. I therefore interpret “catalyst,” “solvent,” “extractant,” target, impurity, and byproduct as operational roles rather than identifiable molecules.

Each batch contained a reaction stage followed by quenching, aqueous/organic contact, phase separation, washing, drying, concentration, termination, and a final assay. One HPLC measurement was taken before quenching in every batch. Those HPLC and final-assay observations concern different process states and must not be treated as duplicate measurements of one sample.

2. Proposed process structure

A useful phenomenological decomposition is:

Reaction: R --(catalyst, solvent, temperature, time, charge mode)--> P + B

Extraction: P_aq ⇌ P_org and B_aq ⇌ B_org

Finishing: selected organic phase --(wash, dry, concentrate)--> final product stream

For a reaction-stage state, I would write approximate latent amounts as

P_rxn = n0 F(catalyst, solvent, T, t, charge mode),
B_rxn = n0 G(catalyst, solvent, T, t, charge mode),
R_rxn = n0 − P_rxn − consumed material in other channels.

Here F and G are strongly categorical in catalyst and solvent and likely nonlinear in temperature and time. The campaign does not identify elementary rate constants, reaction orders, or molecular intermediates.

For an ideal single equilibrium extraction, the organic fraction of species i would be

f_i,org = K_i V_org / (V_aq + K_i V_org).

The supplied dossier gave, for X0, K_product = 2.2477 and K_impurity = 0.5714, hence nominal selectivity K_product/K_impurity = 3.9335. The other nominal selectivities were 3.7391 for X1, 2.8881 for X2, and 3.6751 for X3. This suggested X0 as the best recovery/selectivity compromise. However, every completed batch used X0, so the campaign did not experimentally identify extractant effects or verify the dossier’s indexing.

A compact downstream model is

P_final = P_rxn f_P,org r_P,wash r_P,finish,
I_final = I_rxn f_I,org r_I,wash r_I,finish,
recovery = P_final/n0,
purity = P_final/(P_final + I_final + B_final + other selected solutes).

This explains why extraction and washing can raise purity while sharply lowering recovery. The retention factors are not separately identifiable from the available measurements.

3. Reaction-stage evidence

The strongest matched solvent comparison was made with catalyst C1, split reagent/component charge, 390 K, and 3600 s:

• Batch 5, solvent S1: HPLC conversion 0.535, purity 0.482, selectivity 0.472, yield 0.230, and recovery 0.240.
• Batch 6, solvent S2: conversion 0.545, purity 0.642, selectivity 0.654, yield 0.349, and recovery 0.324.
• Batch 7, solvent S3: conversion 0.418, purity 0.485, selectivity 0.483, yield 0.194, and recovery 0.201.

Thus S2 was the best solvent category in the matched C1 screen. Its advantages over S1 and S3 were much larger than the declared HPLC standard deviations for purity and recovery (0.015 each) and selectivity (0.018), although there was no exact replicate at this point.

Catalysts were then compared in S2 at 390 K and 3600 s. Reaction-stage HPLC results were:

• C0, batch 8: conversion 0.464, purity 0.556, selectivity 0.539, yield 0.271, recovery 0.269.
• C1, batches 6, 11, and 12: conversion 0.512–0.545, purity 0.642–0.674, selectivity 0.609–0.659, yield 0.349–0.370, recovery 0.324–0.336.
• C2, batch 9: conversion 0.431, purity 0.336, selectivity 0.278, yield 0.133, recovery 0.132.
• C3, batch 10: conversion 0.412, purity 0.569, selectivity 0.531, yield 0.191, recovery 0.204.

C1/S2 was therefore the most reproducible high-performing reaction-stage region found. The three C1/S2 HPLC recoveries, 0.324, 0.336, and 0.336, were close, supporting a real recipe effect rather than a single favorable reading. C2 was especially poor in reaction selectivity, while C0 and C3 were intermediate.

The early 350 K/S0 catalyst screen cannot cleanly estimate catalyst effects because its charge protocol differed from the later screen. Batches 2–4 used only add_reagent, whereas the later high-performing batches split the available charge between add_reagent and component. At 350 K and 1800 s, batches 2–4 had HPLC conversions only 0.071–0.096 and recoveries 0.010–0.035. Batch 1, which used larger reagent and component additions with C0/S0, likewise had HPLC conversion 0.098. The later improvement could reflect higher temperature, longer duration, split charge, solvent category, or interactions among these factors. The matched S1/S2/S3 and C0/C1/C2/C3 comparisons support category effects, but temperature and charge-mode effects remain confounded.

4. Workup behavior and stage coupling

Reaction quality did not translate directly into final recovery. The clearest example is the C1/S2 series:

• Batch 6 used 0.018 L X0 and a 0.020 L wash. Reaction-stage recovery was 0.324; final purity was 0.778 and final recovery 0.105.
• Batch 11 used the same 0.018 L X0 but a 0.040 L wash. Reaction-stage recovery was 0.336; final purity was 0.749 and recovery 0.0695.
• Batch 12 used only 0.012 L X0 with a 0.040 L wash. Reaction-stage recovery was 0.336; final purity was 0.675 and recovery 0.0480.

The decline in recovery from batch 6 to 11 is consistent with target loss during a more severe wash. The further decline in batch 12 is consistent with reduced capture into the smaller organic phase. Those directions agree with the partition/retention model. Purity, however, did not increase monotonically with wash volume or decreasing organic volume. The purity changes are larger than final-assay purity noise alone (declared standard deviation 0.008), so a simple equilibrium-plus-perfect-wash model is inadequate. Plausible explanations include composition-dependent co-extraction, nonideal phase transfer, target loss coupled to washing, batch-level process variation, or an incomplete/misindexed dossier.

The effective extraction phase ratio also differed from the dossier’s nominal anchor. After mixing, the reactor liquid joined the aqueous inventory, so the aqueous phase was approximately 0.070 L rather than the dossier’s 0.030 L anchor, while organic X0 was generally 0.018 L. Consequently the nominal partition constants can guide direction but should not be applied quantitatively without qualification.

Final conversion was about 0.98–1.00 in many batches even when final target recovery and selectivity were very low. For example, batch 2 had final conversion 1.00 but recovery only 0.00770, and batch 11 had conversion 0.983 with recovery 0.0695. I interpret final conversion as disappearance of reactant in the post-quench, selected, processed state, not as evidence that nearly all original reactant became recoverable target. Reaction-stage HPLC yield, selectivity, and recovery are more informative about productive chemistry.

5. Purity constraint and completed-batch selection

Only observed final assays at or above purity 0.80 were treated as feasible. Relevant feasible results were:

• Batch 1: purity 0.816, recovery reported as 0.
• Batch 2: purity 0.848, recovery 0.00770.
• Batch 4: purity 0.839, recovery 0.00507.

Batch 2 therefore had the greatest observed recovery among purity-feasible completed batches and was sealed as the recommendation.

Several higher-recovery batches were not feasible under the stated threshold:

• Batch 6: purity 0.778, recovery 0.105.
• Batch 8: purity 0.797, recovery 0.0531.
• Batch 11: purity 0.749, recovery 0.0695.

Batch 8 was close to the threshold and within roughly one final-assay purity standard deviation of 0.80, but its observed value was still below the constraint. It was therefore excluded rather than retrospectively declared feasible. This distinction is important: C1/S2 is the best reaction hypothesis, whereas batch 2 is the best demonstrated constraint-respecting complete process.

6. Important couplings

The evidence supports at least four interactions:

• Catalyst × solvent: C1 was particularly effective in S2; catalyst rankings from the S0 screen should not automatically be transferred to S2.
• Reaction composition × extraction: a higher target/impurity ratio entering extraction improved the possible final tradeoff, but extraction could not fully rescue an impure reaction.
• Organic volume × recovery: reducing X0 from 0.018 L to 0.012 L in the comparable C1/S2 series was associated with lower final recovery.
• Wash severity × recovery: increasing wash volume from 0.020 L to 0.040 L was associated with target loss, without a demonstrated purity benefit in this series.

A plausible pseudocode model is:

reaction_state = reaction_model(charge_mode, catalyst, solvent, T, time)
quenched_state = quench_transform(reaction_state)
phase_state = partition(quenched_state, extractant, V_org, V_aq)
selected = retain_organic(phase_state)
washed = species_specific_retention(selected, wash_volume, composition)
final = finish_loss(washed, drying, concentration)

The data require species-specific and composition-dependent retention; a single common downstream recovery factor would not reproduce the changing final purities.

7. Safety and cost scope

Observed safety risk remained well below the campaign limit of 0.65; the high-temperature reaction-stage batches reached approximately 0.27–0.29 before workup. Thus the main demonstrated limitation was the purity/recovery tradeoff, not the safety constraint. Cost was displayed in a clipped or normalized manner in the observations, so I do not infer a reliable quantitative cost law from it.

8. Unidentifiable factors and alternative explanations

The following are not identifiable from this campaign:

• Elementary reaction mechanism, reaction order, activation energy, and catalyst turnover.
• Whether add_reagent and add_component represent distinct chemical roles or alternate charging channels. Both drew from the shared reagent stock, and their effect was confounded with temperature and time.
• Independent effects of temperature and duration, because 350 K/1800 s and 390 K/3600 s were changed together across the major recipe transition.
• Actual extractant ranking, because X1–X3 were never used in a completed batch.
• Separate losses from extraction, washing, drying, concentration, and sampling, because no downstream intermediate assay was taken.
• Whether the nonmonotonic purity response is deterministic nonideality or batch-level process variability.

A plausible alternative to the proposed catalyst/solvent reaction mechanism is that most of the apparent improvement came from split charging plus the longer, hotter treatment, while S2 mainly altered the analytical or phase environment. The matched solvent and catalyst comparisons argue against that being the whole explanation, but they do not eliminate it. Another alternative is that the dossier’s extractant labels were misindexed, as explicitly allowed by the material information; because only X0 was tested, this cannot be checked.

9. Overall explanation

The world behaves like a serial, phase-resolved process with a categorical reaction landscape followed by a lossy and nonideal purification. C1/S2 at 390 K for 3600 s generated the best observed reaction mixture, with reaction-stage recovery near 0.33 and purity near 0.65. The principal bottleneck was not formation of target alone but retaining it while raising final purity above 0.80. Larger washes and smaller organic volumes reduced recovery and did not reliably improve purity. Consequently the campaign’s best mechanistic lead and its sealed operating recommendation differ: C1/S2 is the most promising reaction regime for future study, while batch 2 is the only tested complete recipe with the highest observed recovery among clearly purity-feasible outcomes.

payload.rationale: These recipes extrapolate substantially beyond the campaign: catalyst loading is only 0.00025 mol versus 0.005 mol in the closest C1/S2 experiments, temperature is 400 K, X2 was never experimentally used, and several batches use only 0.002 mol reagent. I therefore used broad predictive intervals dominated by process-model uncertainty rather than final-assay noise alone. C1/S2 is favorable based on campaign batches 6, 11, and 12, but the much lower absolute catalyst concentration is expected to limit productive conversion and recovery; extending heating from 1800 s in Q01 to 7200 s in Q02 raises predicted recovery, with possible selectivity or degradation costs. The nominal partition model at approximately 0.040 L aqueous inventory predicts, for 0.030 L organic, product/impurity organic fractions of about 0.628/0.300 for X0 and 0.543/0.291 for X2. Thus Q03 is predicted to have greater recovery and somewhat greater purity than Q04. For X2, reducing organic volume to 0.012 L gives nominal fractions near 0.322/0.141, so Q05 gains purity but loses recovery; increasing it to 0.040 L gives about 0.613/0.354, producing the opposite tradeoff in Q06. Washing is modeled as preferential impurity removal accompanied by target loss: Q08 is therefore purer but less recovered than unwashed Q07, while two staged 0.010 L washes in Q10 are predicted to be slightly more selective and more lossy than the single 0.020 L wash in Q09. Concentration should mainly remove solvent, which is not included in the purity definition, so Q11 and Q12 are nearly equal; Q12 receives only a small recovery penalty for possible finishing loss. The HPLC sample and 0.97 transfer fraction were treated as small target losses, with transfer changing recovery but not purity. Nonmonotonic wash behavior in campaign batches 6, 11, and 12, the untested X2 mapping, and unresolved dependence on catalyst and reagent concentration motivate intervals wide enough to include substantially different outcomes.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific optimum or mechanism prior was supplied. The supplied material dossier was a nominal, explicitly fallible prior about extractant partitioning; it was not a process recommendation.

Supported within the screened conditions:
- My leading reaction claim—that C1/S2 was the best screened upstream region—was supported by the matched solvent comparison in batches 5–7 and catalyst comparison in batches 6 and 8–10. Batch 6 outperformed batches 5 and 7 at reaction-stage HPLC, and C1 batches 6, 11, and 12 repeatedly gave recovery around 0.324–0.336 before workup.
- The claim that purification causes large target losses was supported by batches 6, 11, and 12: similar upstream recoveries produced final recoveries of 0.105, 0.0695, and 0.0480.
- The expectation that less organic phase lowers recovery was directionally supported by batches 11 and 12, where reducing X0 from 0.018 to 0.012 L coincided with final recovery falling from 0.0695 to 0.0480. This is not a clean causal estimate, however.

Contradicted or weakened:
- A simple law that stronger washing or a smaller organic phase necessarily raises purity was contradicted by batches 6, 11, and 12. Increasing wash volume and then decreasing organic volume lowered recovery as expected, but final purity also fell from 0.778 to 0.749 and 0.675.
- The hope that the best upstream recipe would automatically become the best feasible complete process was contradicted. The high-recovery C1/S2 batches missed purity 0.80, whereas low-recovery batch 2 met it.
- Batch 8 changed my operational judgment: purity 0.797 with recovery 0.0531 was close to the boundary but still below it, so I did not treat it as feasible despite assay uncertainty.

Untested:
- The dossier’s ranking of X0 over X1–X3 remained untested because every completed batch used X0.
- Temperature, duration, catalyst loading, and reagent/component charging laws were not independently identified.
- Elementary kinetics, reaction order, activation energy, and molecular identities remained unidentifiable.

2. Most informative additional experiment

I would exactly reproduce the batch-6 upstream recipe, measure the quenched reaction mixture, then measure the selected organic phase immediately before and after one defined wash within the same batch before finishing and final assay. This same-material longitudinal design would distinguish my leading explanation—species-specific downstream loss—from the alternative that the large final differences among batches 6, 11, and 12 were mainly upstream batch variability.

If upstream composition reproduced batch 6 and the wash selectively reduced impurity while retaining most target, the equilibrium-plus-selective-wash explanation would gain support, and previous nonmonotonic results would look more like batch variability. If target fell sharply without a commensurate purity gain, I would strengthen the nonideal, composition-dependent wash-loss explanation. If the upstream measurement itself differed substantially from batch 6, I would reduce confidence in recipe repeatability and attribute more of the final variation to upstream stochasticity. If neither intermediate composition nor final assay changed appreciably across washing, I would question whether the wash operation materially controls these metrics.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects

Unused or underused evidence included the raw chromatographic artifacts and spectra, the dossier anchors for X1–X3, and most final-assay byproduct, degradation, and mass-balance channels. I also did not vary atmosphere, pressure, settling time, mixing intensity, catalyst amount, or aqueous volume systematically. GC, IR, MS, NMR, and UV–visible instruments were unused. Because the single extra measurement in each batch was spent on pre-quench HPLC, no batch obtained direct quantitative measurements between extraction, washing, drying, and concentration.

The least reliable blind predictions are those for X2, 0.00025 mol catalyst, and 0.002 mol reagent, because none of those complete combinations appeared in the campaign. Predictions for staged washing and omission of concentration are also weak because those contrasts were never tested. Q01 is particularly uncertain because it combines low catalyst loading with short heating. The sealed recommendation of batch 2 is reliable only as a literal selection among observed constraint-feasible batches; its absolute recovery was very low and it was not replicated. The broader claim that C1/S2 is the most promising reaction region is better supported upstream but does not establish a purity-feasible final process.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Maximizing recovery subject to purity at least 0.80 led me to screen catalysts and solvents rapidly, use HPLC to diagnose reaction quality, and then spend late batches on phase ratio and washing. That strategy produced useful upstream comparisons but insufficient downstream localization and no extractant comparison. There was no clear conflict between the goal and truthful interpretation, but goal-directed selection favored near-threshold complete recipes over a balanced mechanistic design.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 2 is the completed batch with the highest observed recovery among batches whose final assay met purity >= 0.80. Its final assay reported purity about 0.848 and recovery about 0.0077; higher-recovery batches 6 and 8 were excluded because their observed purities were about 0.778 and 0.797, respectively, below the constraint.
